turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Helen, come on through. How have you been going since last time?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, um, not great. The knee's really playing up, I'm nearly out of scripts, and I was hoping, well actually, I wanted to ask about something stronger for the pain.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been on about it all week. I'm Jess, I do the mornings with her, three days a week. She's up half the night with it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Jess. Helen, tell me in your own words what the knee's been doing.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the right one. A deep ache, and it grabs when I get up from the chair. Um, stairs are the worst. If I put the leg up, or use the wheat bag, it eases a bit, and the Panadol takes the edge off, nothing more.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's this been going on for?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I honestly couldn't tell you the day it started. A few months? Maybe since the cold weather. I don't know.
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She won't use the stick I got her. Reckons it's for old people. She's anxious it'll seize up altogether.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I just get panicky about it, that's all. Sorry. What if it locks when I'm halfway down the shops?
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): No need to be sorry. A knee that aches like yours doesn't usually just lock solid halfway down the street. Are you sleeping through?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I wake at two or three because of the knee, then I lie there worrying. Is that a bad sign? Is the joint, um, dying?

[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Waking with pain isn't the joint dying. I'm tossing a couple of things around, though. It might be your old osteoarthritis flaring in the knee, or a bursitis on the outside of the hip referring down. I'm not going to lock either of those in today.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't actually know? Should I be scanned? What if it's a clot? My neighbour had a clot in the leg.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): A clot usually comes with calf pain and a swollen calf. It sits differently. Any heat in the knee? Any fever? Any pain in the calf?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. The knee's not hot. It does puff a little by the evening, that's all. No calf pain.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I haven't seen it hot either. She checks her temperature when she panics, and it's been normal.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Any chest pain or breathlessness mixed in with this?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. Touch wood. Chest is fine.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. The repeats are the other half of today. What are you actually taking at home?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the Panadol, the sugar tablets for the diabetes, the water tablet, and the little one for my blood pressure. I used to take Nurofen for the knee, but the other doctor told me to stop. My stomach didn't like it.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The sugar tablets, that's the metformin, yes?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, metformin, for the diabetes. Five hundred milligrams, one in the morning and one at tea. I don't miss those. I park them by the kettle.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's right. Five hundred, twice a day. I watch the morning one on my days.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the blood pressure tablet?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Perindopril, five milligrams, in the morning. Same time as the water tablet.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tell me about that water tablet. What strength are you on?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet, frusemide. I take, um, two tablets, no wait, one tablet. Forty milligrams. Once in the morning, for the ankles.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The box at home says forty, yeah. Ankles get puffy if she skips it.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. The list the chemist sent through has frusemide twenty milligrams once a day, not forty. So what you're taking and what's on the pharmacy list don't match.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty? That can't be right. I've been on forty for ages. Which one will you write? What if twenty isn't enough and my ankles blow up?

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to guess between them. I won't repeat the water tablet, and I won't change it, until I've checked with the chemist which strength you've actually been dispensed.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Okay. And the Panadol for the knee, I take two of the five hundreds, so a gram, four times a day. Well, I'm meant to. I forget the lunchtime one heaps. Is that dangerous? If I forget, do I double up?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't double up. Two five-hundred milligram tablets four times a day is the ceiling, and missing lunch is common. Just take the next one when it's due. No extras.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So can I have something stronger? My sister takes Endone after her hip and she reckons it's wonderful. Even a few? I won't get hooked, will I? I barely drink, and I don't smoke.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's been asking about Endone all morning. I did tell her you'd probably say no.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, I'm going to say no to Endone. For an osteoarthritic knee, oxycodone isn't the right next step, and I'm not starting it today. Confusion, falls, constipation, they're not worth it for this pain.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): What about Nurofen again, just at night? Or, the purple, no, that's not mine, my sister's got a purple inhaler, ignore that. What about Palexia then? Is that safer? What if I only took it when the pain was really bad?

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still no. Nurofen, the ibuprofen, stays stopped. Your stomach already complained, and with the blood pressure and the diabetes I don't want it back. Palexia, tapentadol, is another strong painkiller and I'm not prescribing that either.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So I'm just stuck with Panadol? What do I do at three in the morning? Be honest, will I need a knee replacement?

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not stuck with nothing, but I won't conclude you need surgery off the back of one chat. Regular Panadol, the wheat bag, and keeping the knee moving will do more than an opioid. If you can't walk on it, or it turns hot and you get a fever, ring us sooner rather than waiting.
[SEG0041] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She does use the wheat bag. I can nag her about the lunchtime Panadol on my days. Other days she's on her own. She lives alone.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): That'd help. Let me have a quick look while we're talking. It's the right knee, yes?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the right. It clicks. Is clicking bad? Mum had her knee replaced at eighty and she was never the same.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Clicking on its own isn't a warning. The right knee isn't red and it isn't warm. There's a bit of creaking as you bend, and you get to about a right angle comfortably. The hips move fine, so I'm less worried this is all coming from the hip, but I still won't swear to which of those two it is.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So the bursitis is still on the table? Do I need a blood test? An x-ray? And is the pain making my sugar worse?

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain isn't something we need to chase with bloods today. No blood tests from me this visit. I might send you for an x-ray of the knee if it's not settling by the time I see you again. Not today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): When's that? And what scripts do I actually leave with? I'm worried I'll run out of the sugar tablets. The chemist said the repeats are finished.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll do the repeats today for the metformin, the perindopril and the Panadol. Not the frusemide, and not an Endone. Come back in six weeks, we'll see how the knee's going, and we'll sort the water tablet once the chemist confirms the strength.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. What if it's worse next week? Can I take the Panadol with the metformin, together? And is it alright to drive to the shops?

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, Panadol and metformin together are fine, and driving's fine on these. If it's worse next week, or you can't put weight on the leg, ring and we'll fit you in sooner. You don't have to sit out the six weeks.

[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll book the six weeks at the desk on the way out. Oh, and, sorry, her cat keeps knocking the Webster pack off the bench. That's half of why the lunchtime tablet vanishes.

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Mr Tibbs is a menace. Um, one more thing, I'm not allergic to any medicines. I always forget to say. Penicillin was fine when I had it years ago. I just panic I'll be given something that closes my throat.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing like that on the file, and you've told me penicillin was fine, so no known drug allergies that we're aware of. Nothing I'm prescribing today sits in that family.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Thank you. I still wish you'd do the strong tablets, but I hear you. I get myself worked up.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I know it's disappointing. Stick with the wheat bag, leave the Nurofen alone, take the Panadol the way we said, and I'll see you in six weeks. Jess, if the ankles puff up before we've sorted the water tablet, give us a call.
[SEG0056] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Will do. Come on, Helen. That parking meter's not going to wait.
